title: BYG610 — Sustainable City Regions
text:
BYG610 — Sustainable City Regions
This site is your course companion for BYG610 at the University of Stavanger. It runs alongside the Canvas course page and is designed to give you richer explanations, conceptual diagrams, and analytical tools than slides alone can offer.

title: BYG610 — Sustainable City Regions
text:
0.1 What the course is about
Regional planning is about making collective decisions over large, complex territories — decisions that affect where people live, how they move, what gets built, and what futures are possible. This course focuses on one of the most interesting challenges in that work: how do planners think about and plan for futures they cannot predict?
We use Rogaland and its live FRAM planning process as our laboratory. FRAM — the County Plan for Regional Development, Land Use and Mobility — is being developed by Rogaland Fylkeskommune right now, pointing towards 2050. This course runs in parallel with that real process, giving you direct access to the people, documents, and debates that shape regional planning practice.

title: 2  Session 1 — Introduction

2.2 What this course is about

Regional planning sits at the intersection of politics, geography, economics, and design. It asks: how do we make collective decisions about complex territories over long time horizons? This course approaches that question through the lens of futures thinking — the set of methods planners use to reason carefully about uncertainty and possibility.

title: 2  Session 1 — Introduction
text:
2.3 The case: Rogaland and FRAM
Rogaland county is in the middle of developing a new comprehensive regional plan — FRAM (Fylkesplan for regional utvikling, areal og mobilitet) — that will guide land use and mobility planning towards 2050. You will follow this process throughout the course.






TipWhy a live case?



Using a real, ongoing planning process as your case means the questions you engage with are not academic abstractions. The people making decisions about Rogaland’s future are accessible — you will meet some of them in Session 3.

title: 3  Session 2 — What is a Region?
text:
3.2 What is a region?
The concept of a “region” is deceptively simple. In practice, planners use at least three different definitions depending on their purpose.


3.2.1 Formal regions
Formal (or administrative) regions are defined by legal boundaries — municipalities, counties, states. In Norway, Rogaland is one of 10 counties (fylker). Its boundaries are legally defined and politically governed by the elected county council (fylkestinget).


3.2.2 Functional regions
Functional regions are defined by flows — commuting, trade, services, infrastructure use. They often cut across administrative boundaries. The Jæren region, for instance, functions as a single labour market stretching across several municipalities.






TipVisualisation: formal vs. functional regions in Rogaland




A map comparing Rogaland’s administrative boundary with commuting-zone catchments will be embedded here.




3.2.3 Perceptual regions
Perceptual regions are defined by identity and cultural meaning — how people feel the region they belong to. These can be surprisingly powerful in planning: the sense of being “from Jæren” or “from Ryfylke” shapes how residents respond to regional plans.
crumbs: 3  Session 2 — What is a Region?

title: 3  Session 2 — What is a Region?

3.3 The Norwegian planning system
Norway’s planning system is hierarchical but not strictly top-down. It operates at three levels, and regional planning sits in the middle — subject to national expectations from above, and needing to guide municipal plans below.








Figure 3.1: The Norwegian planning hierarchy under the Planning and Building Act

ImportantThe binding question



The distinction between binding and non-binding instruments is crucial in Norwegian planning. Most regional plans — including FRAM — are not directly binding on landowners. They guide and require follow-up in municipal plans. Only regional planning provisions (planbestemmelser) are binding, and these cover specific topics rather than the whole plan.

title: 8  Session 7 — Trend & Forecast Scenarios
text:
8.2 What is a forecast scenario?
Trend and forecast scenarios analyse probable futures — they project what is likely to happen if current trajectories continue, using quantitative models and established data. Unlike exploratory scenarios (which embrace uncertainty) or normative scenarios (which articulate desired futures), forecasting assumes that the future is, to a meaningful degree, an extension of the past.
In planning, forecasts are used to:

Set a baseline against which other scenarios are compared
Identify quantifiable risks (flood zones, population pressures, traffic volumes)
Support infrastructure investment decisions that require confident demand estimates
Satisfy legal and procedural requirements in formal plans







TipForecasting is not the same as prediction



A forecast is a conditional statement: if current trends continue, and given these assumptions, we expect X. Good forecasters are explicit about their assumptions and quantify their uncertainty. A forecast is not a promise — it is a structured argument about probability.
crumbs: Part II — Approaches to Regional Futures

title: 8  Session 7 — Trend & Forecast Scenarios
section: 8.4 Forecasting in regional planning: what gets forecast?
text:
8.4 Forecasting in regional planning: what gets forecast?
Regional planning commonly works with forecasts of:

Population — how many people will live in the region, broken down by age, household type, and geography
Housing demand — derived from population and household formation forecasts
Transport demand — trips by mode, origin-destination patterns, road/transit capacity needs
Climate and hazard — flood extent, storm surge, sea level rise at defined return periods

The workshop for this session uses flood and storm surge scenarios from Rogaland as the forecast case — these are regulatory forecasts produced by the Norwegian Environment Agency and NVE that municipalities must account for in their plans.
crumbs: Part II — Approaches to Regional Futures

title: 8  Session 7 — Trend & Forecast Scenarios
text:
8.5 Case: reading Rogaland’s flood forecasts
The workshop uses three forecast scenarios (see the worksheet on Canvas):

200-year flood with climate change projections — fluvial flood extent accounting for increased precipitation
200-year storm surge with sea level rise (2100) — coastal inundation under a high-end sea level rise scenario
Combined flood + storm surge — worst-case compounding scenario







NoteWorkshop task



For each scenario, you will: (1) read the flood/surge map and identify which areas are inundated; (2) assess what this means for neighbourhoods, infrastructure, and critical functions; (3) identify three concrete land use or transport adaptation actions. Use the worksheet (Canvas → Session 7 materials).










Figure 8.2: Illustration of how uncertainty grows in longer-range climate forecasts. The envelope represents the spread across climate model scenarios.
crumbs: Part II — Approaches to Regional Futures

title: 8  Session 7 — Trend & Forecast Scenarios
text:
8.6 The limits of forecasting
Forecasting works well when systems are stable and well-understood — demographic trends over 10–20 years, physical processes with known parameters. It works poorly when:

The system may undergo structural change (energy transition, digital disruption)
The planning horizon is long (30–50 years)
Political choices — not just trends — will shape the outcome
Uncertainty is deep rather than quantifiable

This is exactly why forecasting is the start of the scenario planning sequence, not the end. The exploratory scenarios in Session 8 are designed to challenge the assumptions embedded in the trend forecast.






ImportantA note on the FRAM context



FRAM’s knowledge base includes a range of quantitative analyses — population projections, transport models, climate hazard maps. As you read FRAM documents, notice which claims are forecast-based and which involve value judgements. The distinction matters for understanding what the plan can and cannot defend.
crumbs: Part II — Approaches to Regional Futures

title: 12  Assignment Overview
text:
12.2 Required structure
Your assignment must follow this structure:

Front page — title, course name/number, full name(s), student number(s)
Table of contents
Introduction and problem area — what is the issue, why does it matter?
Research question(s) — precise, answerable, scoped to your method
Literature review and theory — what do scholars say? What conceptual framework guides you?
Methodology — which futures method(s) are you using and why? How did you apply them?
Case description — what is the specific Rogaland context you are analysing?
Analysis — this is the core: applying your method to your question
Conclusion — what did you find? What does it mean for planning?
References
Appendices (if needed)

Detailed guidance for each section is in Assignment Instructions.

title: 12  Assignment Overview
text:
12.3 Choosing your research question
Your question should be:

Spatial — it concerns a territory, a place, a planning challenge in Rogaland
Futures-oriented — it cannot be answered by description alone; it requires reasoning about uncertainty or possibility
Methodologically tractable — you can actually apply one of the course methods to it
Scoped — not so broad that 4,500 words cannot do it justice

See Research Questions for examples and a step-by-step guide to sharpening your question.

title: 12  Assignment Overview
text:
12.4 Which method to choose
You are not required to use all four methods. One well-applied method is better than four superficially mentioned ones. The choice depends on your question:



If your question is about…
Consider…




What is likely to happen (baseline)
Trend/forecast scenario


What could happen under uncertainty
Exploratory scenarios


What should happen (values, vision)
Normative scenarios


How to get from a desired future to the present
Backcasting


Comparing alternative trajectories
Trend + exploratory in sequence



See Methodology Guide for detailed guidance on applying each method in a written assignment.
